newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Schuessel pushes for NATO bid decision.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Schuessel pushes for NATO bid decision.

text.p: Austrian Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schussel on Thursday applauded a deal between Russia and NATO and gave a clear hint he favoured Austria's membership of the Western military alliance.
"The agreement between Russia and NATO is an historic document...It is the birth certificate of a new NATO," Schuessel said in a foreign policy speech.
"For us Austrians this is a huge opportunity and we should seize it and not miss it," he said.

The deal with Moscow outlining a new political and military relationship allows NATO to proceed with plans for its eastwards expansion. The first ex-communist states to join are expected to be the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.

Schuessel's speech marked the 42nd anniversary of Austria's state treaty, which came into force as the four World War Two victors -- the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France -- pulled their troops out of Austria in 1955.
The Kremlin agreed to withdraw its soldiers only if Vienna enshrined neutrality in its constitution.
Straddling the East and West blocs and surrounded to the north, south and east by communist states during the Cold War, Austria never questioned its neutral status.

This taboo was broken following the fall of communism in Eastern Europe in 1989 and the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991. The debate over joining a military alliance intensified after Austria joined the European Union in 1995.

NATO membership has now begun to split the government coalition with Schussel's conservative People's Party broadly backing entry and Chancellor Viktor Klima's dominant Social Democrats against membership.
Conservative Defence Minister Werner Fasslabend caused a stir back home when he said in Paris on Tuesday that it was only a matter of time before the Alpine republic applied to join NATO.
The Social Democrats immediately rejected suggestions Austria should give up its neutrality but the far-right Freedom Party, staunch backers of NATO entry, urged the conservatives to remain firm.

The far right said that they and the conservatives would have an overall majority in parliament to vote in NATO membership but an alliance over such a sensitive issue would force a government collapse.

Schuessel said at NATO headquarters in Brussels last month that his country should seriously consider applying for membership but backtracked on returning home, saying he was speaking as a conservative politician not foreign minister.
On Thursday, he was less reluctant to indicate the direction he and his party would like to follow:
"My position is clear -- the highest degree of effective security for Austria with, of course, mutual defence obligations," he said.
"Since we take over the EU presidency in the second half of 1998, it must be unmistakably clear what Austria is opting for," he added.
He said adopting neutrality 42 years ago was the right decision at the right time for the country's security.
Klima's Social Democrats have adopted a wait-and-see policy but Schuessel warned against wasting time over future defence arrangements.
"As Napoleon once said: Austria is always one year, one army and one idea too late," Schuessel added.
